item.content:encoded:

US and South Korea warn of Gunra ransomware targeting govt agencies — Must Read

U.S. and South Korean agencies warned that Gunra ransomware is targeting government and critical infrastructure organizations worldwide, exploiting Fortinet flaws and exposed remote access to gain entry. Defenders are urged to patch internet-facing systems, segment networks, and keep offline backups as the group expands through a RaaS affiliate program.

  • U.S. federal agencies and South Korea's National Policy Agency warned government and critical infrastructure organizations worldwide to secure their systems against Gunra ransomware attacks.
  • The joint advisory said Gunra first emerged in April 2025 as a double-extortion ransomware variant derived from leaked Conti ransomware source code.
  • Gunra actors have attacked Fortinet firewalls by exploiting CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 in FortiOS and FortiProxy software.
  • Since January 2026, Gunra has launched a ransomware-as-a-service affiliate program and recruited initial access brokers, penetration testers, and ethical hackers.
  • The U.S. and South Korean agencies advised defenders to patch known exploited vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems, segment networks, and make offline backups of their data.

Technologies: firewall, proxy, vpn

Products: fortios, fortiproxy

Vendors: fortinet

Hackers Breach Polish Power Plant Controls via Private Cellular Network and Shut Turbine — Must Read

Attackers breached a Polish heat and power plant through a misconfigured private cellular APN, pivoting from a compromised wind farm to industrial controllers and shutting down a turbine and water treatment system. CERT Polska says the incident shows private APNs must not be treated as trusted isolation and should use client isolation, segmentation, and hardened credentials.

  • Attackers shut down a steam turbine and the process-water treatment system at a Polish combined heat and power plant by entering through a private cellular network used by the local grid operator to reach remote equipment.
  • The plant supplies heat to roughly 50,000 residents, but recovery began while the intruders were still active and customers lost neither heat nor electricity.
  • CERT Polska said the attacker pivoted from a compromised wind-farm network to a controller at the CHP plant because the private APN allowed arbitrary devices on the network to communicate with one another.
  • The WAGO controller reachable through the APN still had default admin credentials, and CERT Polska recommended auditing private APN configurations, enabling client isolation, segmenting traffic, and changing default credentials.
  • According to plant personnel, Siemens S7-300, S7-1200, and S7-1500 controllers were switched to STOP mode and password-protected, while Moxa serial device servers and switches were factory-reset, given changed passwords, and assigned unreachable IP addresses.

Mitiga built FORGE, a multi-agent AI pipeline that drafts and validates cloud detection rules against strict review criteria and real customer telemetry, but still requires human approval before deployment. The key takeaway is that AI can scale detection engineering only when paired with explicit rules, prepared data, adversarial validation, and human oversight.

  • Mitiga built FORGE, an automated detection engineering system that adapts multi-agent AI approaches used for vulnerability hunting to the task of building security detections.
  • FORGE uses a staged pipeline for planning, generating, deduplicating, adversarially validating, red-teaming, reachability testing, and reporting detection candidates.
  • FORGE tests candidate detections against real customer telemetry in Mitiga’s Cloud Security Data Lake, rather than relying only on unit tests.
  • FORGE does not deploy detections automatically; it opens pull requests that humans review and merge.

item.title: Polish Energy Plant OT Breach via Private APN and FortiGate Compromise
item.content:encoded:
Window: 10 Aug 22:00 → 11 Aug 02:00 UTC (4 hours)

Hackers breached a small Polish energy plant via private APN last year — Should Read

Polish CERT says hackers linked to Russia’s Electrum group breached a small Polish heat-and-power plant by moving laterally through a misconfigured private APN, then shut down PLCs controlling a steam turbine and water treatment system. The incident highlights that private APNs should be treated as untrusted networks with client isolation, strict allowlists, and hardened device access.

  • Polish CERT disclosed that hackers compromised a small combined heat-and-power plant in Poland by using a private Access Point Name to access its operational technology network.
  • The attacker switched off programmable logic controllers and protected access with a password, shutting down a steam turbine and the plant’s process-water treatment system.
  • Plant staff restored the impacted systems quickly, so the outage was short-lived and had no impact on the population.
  • Polish CERT determined that the attacker first compromised a FortiGate VPN/firewall at a wind farm and used a Teltonika cellular router to tunnel into a private APN managed by the distribution system operator.
  • Polish CERT said the private APN lacked client isolation, allowing the attacker to scan for and communicate with devices at other facilities.

BdThemes plugins supply-chain hack creates rogue WordPress admins — Must Read

BdThemes’ WordPress plugin ecosystem was hit by a supply-chain compromise where attackers poisoned a remote JSON feed to run malicious JavaScript in admin dashboards, creating hidden rogue administrator accounts. Affected plugins were pulled from WordPress.org while the issue remained under investigation.

  • A threat actor compromised BdThemes’ upstream infrastructure and modified a remote JSON feed delivered to administrators’ browsers to create rogue WordPress administrator accounts.
  • Wordfence researchers said the attacker poisoned a static remote JSON data stream after obtaining write access to the vendor’s storage bucket, exploiting a cross-site scripting flaw in the Biggop Library used by the Biggopti component.
  • The malicious JavaScript used a legitimate administrator’s authenticated session to create rogue admin accounts, and an additional payload called w2.js established persistence through a webshell named emer-run.php by installing a fake plugin.
  • The affected BdThemes plugins were pulled from the WordPress.org directory on August 8 pending investigation, and the issue was listed as unpatched as of publication.
  • Defiant said the earliest possible start of the campaign was June 23, while Wordfence began seeing attacks through its web application firewall on August 7.

Senate Democrats introduce bill to distribute $300 million annually to shore up water system cybersecurity — Should Read

Sens. Adam Schiff and Amy Klobuchar introduced the Water Cyber Shield Act to provide $300 million annually for cybersecurity upgrades to U.S. water and wastewater systems. The bill would expand EPA authority to assess vulnerabilities, require fixes and incident reporting, and coordinate standards with CISA after a wave of attacks on water utilities.

  • Sens. Adam Schiff and Amy Klobuchar introduced the Water Cyber Shield Act, which would allocate $300 million annually for cybersecurity improvements in the water and wastewater sector.
  • The bill would give the Environmental Protection Agency authority to conduct cybersecurity assessments of water and wastewater systems and require corrective actions when vulnerabilities are found.
  • The legislation follows recent cyberattacks on at least 30 water and wastewater systems in about 12 states, which experts believe were launched by groups connected to Iran’s military.
  • Water and wastewater systems would need to assess cybersecurity risk as part of resilience planning and comply with incident reporting requirements under the forthcoming Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act.
  • The EPA would coordinate with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on threat information and cybersecurity standards, and a technical advisory committee would be created to develop those standards.

China-linked hackers turning popular cybersecurity tool into ransomware launchpad, Microsoft warns — Must Read

Microsoft warns that China-linked Storm-1175 is likely exploiting a critical N-able N-central flaw to turn MSP remote management servers into launchpads for rapid downstream ransomware attacks using the new StormEncryptor strain. Organizations running N-central should urgently apply the latest hotfixes and reduce exposure, as earlier patches were bypassed and many instances remain vulnerable.

  • Microsoft Threat Intelligence warned that the China-linked Storm-1175 group began deploying a new ransomware strain called StormEncryptor on August 2.
  • Microsoft said Storm-1175 is likely exploiting CVE-2026-18577, a critical vulnerability in N-able’s N-central remote monitoring and management console.
  • Huntress said CVE-2026-18577 allows attackers with no credentials to gain full administrative control of an N-central server, which can provide access to every endpoint the server manages.
  • N-able said the vulnerability was first detected in a zero-day attack on July 31 and issued emergency hotfixes on August 2 and August 6 after attackers bypassed an initial patch.
  • Huntress found that more than half of reachable N-central cloud servers across its partner base were still unpatched, along with 28.6% of self-hosted instances.

TrueConf Server Flaws Exploited to Replace Client Installers with PhantomCore — Must Read

Head Mare exploited chained flaws in unpatched TrueConf Server instances to replace legitimate client installers with PhantomCore-infected versions, giving attackers SYSTEM-level access and persistent web shell control. The flaws are patched in newer TrueConf Server releases, so affected organizations should update immediately.

  • Kaspersky detected July 2026 attacks in which the threat actor Head Mare exploited chained flaws in unpatched TrueConf servers targeting Russian companies in instrumentation, electronics, transport, energy, IT, and software development sectors.
  • The TrueConf attack exploited KLCERT-26-057 and KLCERT-26-058 to achieve arbitrary code execution with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges and replace the file "...\public\js\locale.php" with a web shell.
  • The attackers used the TrueConf web shell to collect information about IT infrastructure, gain privileged access to the TrueConf database, and replace the original TrueConf Client installer with an infected version containing the PhantomCore backdoor and remote access trojan.
  • Kaspersky said the web shell also delivered PhantomGraph, which uses SysExcSvc.dll and SysReadSvc.dll modules and Microsoft OneDrive as command-and-control storage.
  • Kaspersky also reported a separate HelloNet campaign abusing the ViPNet update mechanism to load HelloInjector, HelloProxy, HelloExecutor, HelloCleaner, and HelloBackdoor against Russian government, energy, transport, education, and logistics sectors.

Products: trueconf-server, trueconf-client, vipnet, microsoft-onedrive, havoc-c2

New Passkey Attacks Can Recover Synced Private Keys or Bypass Phishing-Resistant MFA — Should Read

Recent research showed that passkeys can be bypassed or abused when surrounding systems expose signed authentication data, mishandle synced key protection, or allow malware in an active Windows session to use hardware-backed credentials. The core cryptography remains intact, but defenders should patch Windows, harden WebAuthn validation, and treat endpoints and passkey stores as high-value credential targets.

  • Three separate research efforts demonstrated ways to defeat passkey protections without breaking the cryptography behind them.
  • SpecterOps showed a Windows and Microsoft Entra ID chain that reused signed authentication material exposed by Windows to impersonate privileged users while satisfying phishing-resistant multifactor authentication.
  • Unit 42 showed attacks against Google Password Manager in Chrome on Windows, including a method called Golden Pass-ta-key that can recover private keys for a victim's synced passkeys by targeting the Security Domain Secret.
  • Dirk-jan Mollema showed that malware already running in a signed-in Windows session can use a hardware-bound Windows Hello for Business key without prompting the user for a fresh PIN or biometric check.
  • Microsoft has issued a security update for CVE-2026-34348 and said it applied mitigations for the reported issue involving passkey relay assertions.

Technologies: operating-system, browser, identity-provider, iam, mfa

Products: windows, microsoft-entra-id, windows-event-logging-service, windows-hello-for-business, google-password-manager, google-chrome, yubikey

Vendors: microsoft, google, yubico

Known Sender, Perfect Auth, Confirmed Malicious Link — Should Read

A fully authenticated vendor CRM reply in a real healthcare service thread was quarantined because it contained a URL independently scored as malicious, showing that SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and sender familiarity do not prove message safety. Release decisions should evaluate the flagged content itself, not rely on known-sender trust.

  • A logistics coordinator at a regional U.S. healthcare system received a reply to a genuine service request from a long-standing equipment vendor, and the message included the correct case reference and instrument serial numbers.
  • The email came from the vendor’s own corporate domain through its CRM sending stream, with SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication all passing.
  • One hyperlink in ordinary paragraph text pointed to hxxps://process[.]to/, which was recorded as malicious by the link scanner and corroborated by an external sandbox score of 66 out of 100.
  • The message was quarantined on arrival and two more times on repeat delivery attempts, and three release requests based on the sender being known were all denied.
  • The article states that authentication confirms sender identity and message integrity but does not determine whether a URL inside the message is safe.

Companies deploying AI agents that EU users can interact with are likely covered by the EU AI Act, even though the Act does not explicitly use the word “agent.” At minimum they must meet Article 50 transparency duties, and higher-risk or model-modifying uses can trigger broader provider and high-risk system obligations.

The key lesson is that authenticated, payload-free emails can still be phishing when the real payload is an off-channel contact request.
